::: {.section-card}
### Quantifying demand and supply

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="48%"}
<p class="overview-panel-kicker">Estimating vacancies from job postings (OJV vs OJP)</p>
<ul class="overview-list">
<li>Postings with an <strong>explicit vacancy count</strong> (6.7%) → taken at face value</li>
<li>Postings stating <strong>“multiple” positions</strong> without a number (8.9%) → coded as <strong>2 vacancies</strong> (conservative)</li>
<li><strong>Single-position</strong> postings (84.4%) → coded as <strong>1 vacancy</strong></li>
</ul>
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
<p class="overview-panel-kicker">Training data — scope and limitations</p>
<ul class="overview-list">
<li>Training records include only <strong>minimum and maximum capacity</strong> per service — actual participant numbers are unavailable</li>
<li>Without attendance distributions, estimating total participants is not feasible</li>
<li>Analysis therefore focuses on the <strong>structure of training offerings</strong>: course types and skills taught</li>
</ul>
<p class="overview-foot">Skills are extracted from learning outcomes and service descriptions and mapped to ESCO.</p>
:::
:::

::: {.framing-callout}
Both sides are reduced to the same unit — the share of each skill group in demand vs. in supply. Skill analyses focus on <strong>composition</strong>, not on scaling postings to vacancies or courses to participants. What matters is that skill shares are measured consistently on both sides.
:::

:::

::: {.section-card}
### Why Pracuj.pl as the single source for online vacancies

Online job-posting research faces a methodological trade-off: (a) a single dominant portal with known sectoral selection bias, vs. (b) multi-source aggregation with noise from imperfect cross-source deduplication.

Cross-source deduplication is the core technical challenge in (b). The same vacancy may appear with slightly different titles, descriptions, or layouts across portals; identifying matches requires a similarity threshold that inevitably either over-merges (losing real vacancies) or under-merges (inflating counts).

**Empirical context:** Lightcast reports ~2.24M Polish postings in 2025 vs. ~731k unique postings on Pracuj.pl alone. Broader coverage explains part of the gap, but a 3× ratio is hard to reconcile with unique vacancies — likely reflecting residual duplicates.

::: {.framing-callout}
This report uses a single-source approach based on Pracuj.pl — Poland's largest commercial job portal, with strong coverage of white-collar, IT, and specialist roles. We do not claim full-population coverage of online vacancies; Pracuj.pl is treated as a high-quality, internally consistent sample of market labour demand.
:::
